# Incident Report — MTA 2026-01-31 Traffic Analysis

## Evidence Reviewed
- `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 frames, 26.4 MB). No separate IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence folder; all findings below are derived directly from packet analysis with `tshark`.

## Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 10.1.21.58 | Source of all outbound traffic to external hosts; consistent across ARP, DHCP, NBNS |
| MAC address | 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2 | ARP replies for 10.1.21.58 and DHCP `dhcp.hw.mac_addr` |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-ES9F3ML (workgroup/domain-suffix advertised as WIN11OFFICE) | NBNS name records (`<00>`, `<20>`) for 10.1.21.58; DHCP option 12 hostname; mDNS/DNS PTR query for `DESKTOP-ES9F3ML` |
| Logged-in user | gwyatt | Kerberos `CNameString` (AS-REQ/TGS-REQ client principal name) on the LDAP/Kerberos traffic to the domain controller (10.1.21.2) |

## Malware Family
**Attribution: behavioral (not signature-confirmed).** No malware binary was ever transmitted in cleartext (the payload-sized transfer described below is TLS-encrypted end to end, so no PE/archive was recoverable for hashing), so no static/YARA/AV signature match was possible from this capture alone.

The observed chain matches a **JavaScript-based browser-fingerprinting stealer/loader gate**, consistent with current "fake file-host / ClickFix-style" stealer distribution campaigns (e.g., Lumma-/StealC-class stealer loaders): the victim is funneled through a fake file-hosting portal, a large encrypted archive/installer is pulled down, and shortly after, an in-browser or dropped component performs canvas/WebGL/WebRTC/audio/font fingerprinting and attempts to upload a results archive to a "set_agent" C2 API using an `id`/`token`/build-ID scheme.

## Infection Timeline (capture-relative time)

1. **t≈45.9s** — DNS resolves `media.megafilehub4.lat` → 104.21.48.156 and `hiyter.com` → 104.21.22.231 (fake file-hosting-style domains).
2. **t≈48.4s** — DNS resolves `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` → 104.21.46.67. Host immediately opens a TLS session that transfers **~16 MB in 22.4 seconds** (19,722 packets) — by far the largest single conversation in the capture, consistent with a payload/archive download. Content is TLS-encrypted (SNI shows `cloudflare-ech.com`, indicating TLS 1.3 Encrypted Client Hello via Cloudflare), so the transferred object could not be recovered or hashed from this capture.
3. **t≈90.4s** — DNS resolves `whooptm.cyou` → 62.72.32.156; short encrypted TLS session follows.
4. **t≈92–104s** — Host repeatedly contacts `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49) over HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443):
   - `GET /api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome` (then repeated with `agent=Edge`) — beacon/registration to the C2 panel, once per installed browser.
   - `POST /api/set_agent?...&act=log` with an 8,023/7,975-byte `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body containing a full browser fingerprint: platform, userAgent, WebGL vendor/renderer, a canvas fingerprint PNG (base64), WebRTC candidate probe, screen/hardware/font enumeration, and installed PDF-viewer plugin list.
   - Server response to the log upload: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, body = **`cant open archive 172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip`** — this reveals the C2 panel's expected exfil-archive naming convention: `<victim-public-IP>-<hex build/HWID>.zip`, and confirms the panel is designed to receive and unpack a stolen-data archive (the upload here failed server-side, but the mechanism is unambiguous).
5. **t≈122–127s** — DNS resolves `holiday-forever.cc` → 80.97.160.24 and `communicationfirewall-security.cc` → 104.21.9.36; brief encrypted TLS sessions to each follow. Both are freshly-patterned, low-reputation-style domains contacted only during this infection window, alongside otherwise normal Microsoft/Google/MSN background traffic.

All of the above domains and IPs are distinct from, and interleaved with, ordinary Windows/Edge/Office telemetry and Google/Bing/MSN traffic that makes up the bulk of the capture (background noise, not malicious).

## Indicators of Compromise

**C2 / infrastructure endpoints**
- `153.92.1.49:80` and `153.92.1.49:443` — active stealer log/fingerprint C2 panel (`whitepepper.su`)
- `104.21.46.67:443` — payload/archive delivery host (`arch.filemegahab4.sbs`, fronted by Cloudflare)
- `104.21.48.156:443` — landing/loader host (`media.megafilehub4.lat`)
- `104.21.22.231:443` — associated host (`hiyter.com`)
- `62.72.32.156:443` — associated host (`whooptm.cyou`)
- `80.97.160.24:443` — associated host (`holiday-forever.cc`)
- `104.21.9.36:443` — associated host (`communicationfirewall-security.cc`)

**Malicious domains**
- whitepepper.su (confirmed C2 panel — fingerprint collection + log-upload endpoint)
- arch.filemegahab4.sbs (payload delivery, 16 MB TLS transfer)
- media.megafilehub4.lat
- hiyter.com
- whooptm.cyou
- holiday-forever.cc
- communicationfirewall-security.cc

**Malicious URLs (cleartext, observed in full)**
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log`

**Client/build identifiers**
- Panel client ID: `3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`
- Panel auth token: `842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`
- Referenced exfil archive name (from server error message): `172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip` (build/HWID hex: `038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1`)

**File names / hashes**
- No malware binary or archive was recoverable from the capture — the 16 MB delivery to `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` is TLS-encrypted end to end (Encrypted Client Hello), so no file name or SHA256 could be computed for the payload itself.
- SHA256 hashes were computed for the recoverable cleartext HTTP objects (fingerprint POST bodies, favicon, connectivity-check text) exchanged with `whitepepper.su`, but these are stealer-panel exfil artifacts/noise, not the malware executable, and are not listed as malicious file IOCs.

## Benign Context (excluded from IOCs)
Background Windows/Office/Edge telemetry and consumer app traffic present throughout the capture: `login.microsoftonline.com`, `login.live.com`, `*.events.data.microsoft.com`, `officeapps.live.com`, `ecs.office.com`, `client.wns.windows.com`, `edge.microsoft.com`, `*.msn.com`, `*.google.com`/`googleapis.com`, `bing.com`, `gstatic.com`, `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `adobedtm.com`, `msftconnecttest.com`/`dns.msftncsi.com`, mDNS/LLMNR/SSDP/NBNS local discovery, and normal Kerberos/LDAP/DCE-RPC/SMB2 traffic to the internal domain controller (10.1.21.2).

## Summary
Windows workstation **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** (10.1.21.58, MAC 00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2), logged in as domain user **gwyatt**, was infected after visiting a fake file-hosting site (`media.megafilehub4.lat` / `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`) and pulling down a 16 MB encrypted archive/installer. Within seconds, the host began beaconing to a C2 panel at `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49), registering per-browser (Chrome, then Edge) and uploading detailed browser-fingerprint data intended for an exfil archive named after the victim's public IP and a build ID, with brief follow-on contact to several other low-reputation domains (`whooptm.cyou`, `holiday-forever.cc`, `communicationfirewall-security.cc`, `hiyter.com`). The behavior is consistent with a JavaScript-based stealer/loader fingerprinting-and-exfil gate typical of current commodity infostealer distribution chains; family attribution is behavioral only, as the actual payload was never observed in cleartext.
